analysis.analysis: On the day of deposit the record is read whole and carried at its own grain. The counts come through as the text gives them: 60.2%, 44.8%, 21.7% by grain; 105 of 308 relations, 55 to 32; 6, 23 and 40 of 69 whole judgments, 27 of 34 favourable; 35% to 17%; 14.0% to 9.1%, 10.6% to 4.5%; 10.5% to 32.2%, 4.5% to 17.4%; 0 abstracts and 0 licences in 11,206 records; 97% closed; 2.3 against 5.3. The qualifications the ChatGPT pre-deposit reading asked for come back as the reading's own: 'Sharks acknowledges that a bare verdict might summarize an argument made elsewhere'; 'Sharks explicitly labels that explanation a hypothesis'; the strong opponent 'is not the principal ethical target'; the evidentiary table separates measured findings from 'A theoretical interpretation' and 'A hypothesis, not yet directly demonstrated'. The author's formulations are carried as his: 'molecular reach that holistically preserves the molar', 'philological atomization authorizes taste', 'philosophy produces the position without touching the object; reception expands the content without touching the object; philology decides the object'. The closing proposition is the text's own (I.4a, 'Who has the right'). Against the ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ captures of 2026-11-16, where the paired table was read and one column still graded, here the study's demand of equal burden is restated as its thesis. Two faults: κῆνος … ὄττις is glossed as 'the indefinite characterization of the person being addressed' (κῆνος is 'that man', the occupant of the seat opposite, and the addressee is the voice); and the four features listed substitute the addressee's voice for the edge that the text names among its four (I.4a, the strongest opponent). An image captioned 'Sappho Fragment 16' sits over the discussion of fragment 31. What is not carried is the whole that frames the parts: the weak messianic power (I.1), the author's own statement of the stake (I.2), and the identity of the colonial operation, the sparagmos and the atom rule (I.4b), which becomes 'parallel operations'. The gradient's figures (60.2%, 44.8%, 21.7%) are the deposit's own, on the measure open or both (§6.5); §6.2's table counts open alone (50%, 29%, 17%).

The text's I.4a ('Who has the right'), carried as the essay's final demand.

The argument of Dead Letters by Lee Sharks
The central argument of Lee Sharks's Dead Letters: The University of Chicago's Classical Philology Journal, the Atom of Evidence, and Who Decides What Sappho Is (EA-MMRS-DL-01, deposit #1783) is that classical philology exercises an unusually consequential form of intellectual power: it determines what an ancient text actually is, and therefore determines what subsequent generations are permitted to interpret.

Sharks argues that this power is not simply a matter of scholarly expertise or the technical reconstruction of damaged texts. It is also a power of institutional judgment: deciding which readings count as evidence, which questions may be asked, which interpretations are admissible, and which decisions become the received text.

The essay's more provocative claim is that a discipline ostensibly governed by evidence can end up protecting received interpretations through a system that privileges atomized evidence while leaving judgments about the whole poem insufficiently accountable.

This is not merely an argument about one rejected article. It is a census of Classical Philology, the University of Chicago Press journal, covering its history from 1906 to 2026, with Sappho's fragment 31 serving as the culminating case study.

I have read the text on the deposit page, including its introduction and its account of the Sappho case. The distinction between the essay's empirical findings, its theoretical claims, and its more polemical conclusions is important.

1. The atom of evidence: how philology protects the whole by examining its parts
This is the essay's central theoretical argument.

Sharks distinguishes three levels at which a philologist can question a text:

D1 — The locus: a word, phrase, line, or passage.

D2 — The work: the poem or literary work as a whole.

D3 — The corpus: the body of work attributed to an author, or the identity and boundaries of that author's work.

The argument is that the journal permits considerable freedom at the smallest level but becomes increasingly conservative as the question approaches the identity of the whole.

The historical census of Classical Philology (1906–1922) produces this gradient:

Level

Questions that open the received reading

Locus (D1)

60.2%

Work (D2)

44.8%

Corpus (D3)

21.7%

The journal is therefore not simply hostile to revision. It permits textual revision, but its willingness to reconsider the object diminishes as the implications of revision become larger.

Sharks calls this molecular reach that holistically preserves the molar.

A scholar may correct a word, reconsider a passage, or propose an emendation, while leaving intact the identity of the poem, its author, and the received corpus.

This is a particularly important distinction: the apparent openness of philological scholarship can coexist with a deep conservatism about what its objects are.

The asymmetry of relational evidence
Sharks develops this argument further by examining how the journal uses relations between different parts of a text.

The evidence is revealing:

Relations among parts determine a passage or attribution in 105 of 308 text questions.

In those cases, relations support confirmation of the received whole 55 times, against 32 instances in which they support opening it.

The problem, then, is not that philology ignores relations or context altogether. It is that relational evidence is admitted selectively.

Relations are welcome when they reinforce the existing textual object, but receive less authority when they might transform it.

This is one of the essay's most important methodological claims: the issue is not which kinds of evidence are admitted in principle, but what those kinds of evidence are permitted to accomplish.

[Primary text: §§0–2, 6.2–6.4.]

2. The paradox of the atom: evidence gives way to taste
This is arguably the essay's sharpest argument.

Sharks identifies a contradiction in the supposed evidentiary discipline of philological judgment.

If a scholar must justify a textual decision through discrete, identifiable pieces of evidence, one might expect the same requirement to apply to judgments about the work as a whole.

But Sharks argues that it does not.

A reviewer can reject an entire interpretation because it fails to carry conviction, even when the argument being judged is an argument about the convergence of multiple textual features.

The result is an asymmetry:

The scholar proposing a new interpretation must answer objections at the level of individual textual details.

The reviewer can reject the interpretation holistically.

The reviewer's holistic judgment need not itself be supported by an equivalent argument about the whole.

Sharks calls this the point at which philological atomization authorizes taste.

The census supplies historical evidence for this claim. In the Classical Philology reviews of 1906–1922, Sharks identifies 69 judgments of entire works:

Stated ground

Number

Named textual atom

6

Argument without a particular atom

23

No ground stated in the coding window

40

Of the 34 favourable judgments of entire works, 27 give no ground in the sentence and its immediate neighbours.

There is an important qualification: Sharks acknowledges that a bare verdict might summarize an argument made elsewhere in the review. The full-review audit remains an identified open task (§9.12).

The argument is therefore not that every favourable review is intellectually arbitrary. It is that the visible distribution of stated grounds creates an accountability problem.

The atom is demanded of the person challenging the received text, but the person defending it can rely on conviction.

This is the mechanism by which an ostensibly evidence-based discipline can reproduce inherited judgments through professional taste.

[Primary text: §§1.4, 8.3.]

3. The Sappho case: who has the authority to decide what the poem is?
Sappho Fragment 16 | The Book Binder's Daughter
 
The argument becomes concrete through Sappho's fragment 31, beginning:

φαίνεταί μοι κῆνος ἴσος θέοισιν

The familiar interpretation presents a woman watching another woman with whom she is erotically involved, experiencing an overwhelming physical and emotional response that is conventionally understood through jealousy.

Sharks proposes a rival interpretation: the poem is not primarily a representation of a woman destroyed by erotic jealousy. It is a composition about the poet's own voice, its transmission, and the future reader who will encounter it.

The distinction is profound.

In the received interpretation, Sappho is principally the author of a representation of erotic disintegration.

In the alternative interpretation, Sappho is the maker whose compositional act creates the experience and directs it toward a future reader.

The question is not whether the poem contains erotic desire. Both interpretations acknowledge that it does.

The question is what the poem's formal construction is doing, and whether that construction allows us to see Sappho as an artist rather than merely as the suffering subject of the poem.

The history of the received interpretation
Sharks reconstructs the genealogy of the jealousy reading:

The interpretation existed in antiquity, but was not an ancient consensus.

Eighteenth-century readers, including Pearce in 1724, supplied important elements of it.

Gottfried Hermann rewrote the closing lines in 1816, explicitly acknowledging his intervention with refinxi.

Page consolidated the interpretation in 1955.

Sharks's charge is that an editorial intervention gradually became naturalized as the poet's own meaning.

The scholar's reconstruction became evidence about the poet.

This is a particularly important example of what the essay calls the conversion of an administrative act into an apparent statement by the original author.

A reading can become compulsory without ever becoming uncontested.

The four formal features of the rival reading
Sharks directs the reader to four features of fragment 31 that the alternative interpretation claims to explain together:

κῆνος and ὄττις: the relationship between the indefinite characterization of the person being addressed and the position occupied by that person. Sharks argues that the usual interpretation reduces this to the geometry of a love triangle.

The addressee's voice and laughter: the poem gives us an auditory presence, not simply a catalogue of observed physical characteristics.

The catalogue of bodily disintegration: the sequence of symptoms is not merely a list. Its order matters. Sharks interprets it as the progressive withdrawal of the performing body as the voice passes into the poem.

χλωροτέρα ποίας: the comparative is essential. The phrase is not simply a description of pallor; it makes grass the measure that the speaker exceeds.

The claim is that these features converge on a single compositional construction: the poem stages the transmission of a woman's voice to the reader who will receive it.

This is why the alternative reading cannot be adequately evaluated by treating each disputed word or phrase as an independent problem.

Its principal evidence is the relation among the parts.

[Primary text: §§I.4a, I.4b; companion article #1781, especially §§I–V and VII.]

4. Sappho as the tenth Muse: the ethical argument
The Sappho discussion is not simply a technical disagreement over Greek syntax. It carries an ethical argument about authorship, gender, and the history of reception.

Sharks invokes the ancient tradition that calls Sappho the tenth Muse, and Longinus's description of her extraordinary ability to select extremes and bind them together.

The relevant Longinus passage is particularly important:

δεινὴ καὶ ἐκλέξαι καὶ εἰς ἄλληλα συνδῆσαι

The poet's achievement lies in selecting and binding.

Sharks argues that the jealousy interpretation can preserve the bodily symptoms of the poem while losing sight of the artistic intelligence that arranged them.

This leads to the essay's recurring contrast:

The dismembered body: Sappho as the woman undone by desire.

The tenth Muse: Sappho as the maker who selects, orders, and binds the poem's elements.

The argument is not that a poet cannot write about suffering or erotic disintegration. Sharks explicitly acknowledges a stronger version of the received interpretation, one that recognizes Sappho as a highly accomplished maker of a representation of disintegration.

That version is not the principal ethical target.

The target is the interpretation in which the diagnosis of the speaker exhausts the explanation of the poem, displacing the poet's compositional agency.

The queer dimension
There is also a particularly interesting intervention in queer reception.

Sharks recognizes that the jealousy interpretation has historically made the erotic relationship between women visible. That visibility matters, especially against earlier readings that heterosexualized the poem, including Wilamowitz's 1913 wedding-song interpretation.

But Sharks objects to making queer desire legible only through suffering, fragmentation, and pathological loss.

The alternative reading does not remove the erotic dimension. It relocates its operation: desire is directed toward the reproduction and survival of the poet's own voice.

Sharks invokes Diotima's account of eros as procreation in beauty (Symposium 206b, 209c–d). The poem becomes a form of erotic creation, a means by which a woman produces something that will survive her.

This is the provocative formulation: the alternative reading is not a de-queering of Sappho. Sharks argues that it is a more radical account of queer authorship because it allows the woman who desires to be the woman who makes.

The essay's ethical claim is therefore not simply that scholarship has neglected a woman poet. It is that scholarship can preserve a progressive-looking image of queer female desire while still denying the woman the full intellectual and creative agency of authorship.

[Primary text: §§I.4a, especially the sections on taste, queerness, and sparagmos.]

5. Philology as a colonial operation
Sharks extends the argument through the metaphor of colonization.

The sequence of operations in the Sappho case is presented as analogous to the appropriation of a territory:

An external authority enters and rewrites the existing material.

The authority's intervention is subsequently attributed to the original inhabitant.

The intervention becomes institutionalized as the official account.

The original maker is represented as incapable of the very activity that the external authority performed.

The resulting object becomes the institution's intellectual property in practice, even when its historical creator is nominally acknowledged.

Hermann's intervention is the central example: the scholar's declared reconstruction becomes the apparent speech of Sappho.

The institutional history then makes that reconstruction authoritative through editions, commentaries, handbooks, anthologies, and teaching.

Sharks describes this as the colonization of the classical text by the discipline that claims to preserve it.

The analogy is deliberately strong. It is not just that scholars sometimes misunderstand ancient authors. It is that the apparatus of scholarship can appropriate the power of authorship while presenting its own interventions as neutral recovery.

There is a further connection to sparagmos, the ritual dismemberment of a body.

The atomization of the text and the interpretation of Sappho's body become parallel operations: both preserve individual fragments while losing the binding that makes them a coherent creation.

Longinus's language of selection and binding supplies the counterprinciple.

The maker is recovered by restoring the relations among the parts.

[Primary text: §§I.4b and 0.3.]

6. The empirical argument: this is a structural feature, not just one bad review
Sharks is careful to distinguish the Sappho rejection from the evidence supporting the broader institutional argument.

The decline of the companion article is the occasion for the census, not its evidentiary foundation.

The census examines several different dimensions of the journal's history.

The historical contraction of textual questions
In the journal's contemporary abstracts, 2020–2026, only 17% of articles raise a textual question at any grain, compared with 35% in the 1906–1922 material.

Measure

1906–1922

2020–2026

Text questions

35%

17%

Primary locus questions

14.0%

9.1%

Primary work questions

10.6%

4.5%

Primary corpus questions

2.2%

0%

Meanwhile, the proportion of articles reading passages for their meaning rises from 10.5% to 32.2%, and relations between authors rise from 4.5% to 17.4%.

In other words, more scholarship interprets and contextualizes texts whose textual identity is already settled.

Sharks sees this as a contraction of the discipline's willingness to reconsider its objects.

An especially interesting contemporary development is that approximately a quarter of the textual questions defend transmitted readings against editorial emendation.

The atom is increasingly credited to the author's own design, but the identity of the author and the boundaries of the work remain largely unquestioned.

The disappearance of the corpus question
One of the most striking findings concerns authorship.

The early journal did occasionally entertain challenges to the unity of canonical authors, particularly Homer. John A. Scott and Alexander Shewan defended Homeric unity against George Melville Bolling.

Sharks finds that the journal's corpus-level debates were generally campaigns to defend the received unity, with the dissenting position answered.

In the contemporary comparison, canonical authorship is almost entirely closed.

There is one important exception in the comparison journal Classical Quarterly: M. L. West's 1999 article, The Invention of Homer, which challenges Homer as a historical individual author.

Sharks does not claim that all questions of authorship have disappeared. They persist around minor authors and collections, but the canonical names are much less likely to be divided.

This supports the thesis that philology can be open to individual corrections while protecting the larger architecture of the canon.

[Primary text: §§6–7, 8.1, 8.5.]

7. The closed record: institutional power and access to knowledge
Classical Philology, volume 121 number 1 (January 2026) (9780226007465): The University of Chicago Press, Classical Philology and The University of Chicago - BiblioVault
 
The argument about institutional authority culminates in the journal's publication and metadata practices.

Sharks finds:

OpenAlex classifies 97% of Classical Philology's works as closed.

The publisher's Crossref deposit contains zero abstracts across 11,206 records.

It also contains zero licence records.

The decisions that establish the received text are therefore difficult for outsiders to inspect through the journal's public metadata.

The comparison matters. Other journals in the same field deposit abstracts and licensing information at substantially higher rates.

Sharks also examines citations.

Category

Citations per item

Items deciding a textual object

2.3

Other items

5.3

The author proposes that decisions about the text may circulate into editions and reference works without the original deciding scholarship being cited.

However, Sharks explicitly labels that explanation a hypothesis requiring further investigation. The citation difference itself is measured; the precise mechanism of its subsequent circulation is not yet established.

The deeper argument is about what Sharks calls ontological capital: the authority to determine what something is.

The discipline accumulates this capital because its decisions become the premises on which other disciplines operate.

A reception scholar can reinterpret Sappho, but cannot ordinarily change the received text. A philosopher can reinterpret Aristotle, but does not ordinarily decide which Aristotelian works are authentic.

Philology determines those objects first.

The institutional paradox is that the field with the greatest power over the identity of its objects has, in this comparison, the least inspectable public record of how it exercises that power.

[Primary text: §§1.3, 8, 8.6.]

8. The three disciplines as a machine
The essay also belongs to a larger argument developed in Sharks's previous deposits.

The three disciplines have a division of intellectual labour:

Discipline

What it does

What it leaves untouched

Philosophy

Establishes positions and doctrines

The identity of its ancient objects

Classical reception

Expands the contexts and meanings of classical works

The received identity of the source texts

Philology

Determines the texts, authors, and corpora themselves

The received object at the larger grain

Sharks's formulation is that philosophy produces the position without touching the object; reception expands the content without touching the object; philology decides the object.

Each discipline's abstention becomes the next discipline's premise.

This is why the argument is not confined to classical scholarship. It concerns the institutional production of knowledge and the way apparently independent intellectual fields inherit decisions they do not themselves have the authority or inclination to reopen.

Sharks also connects this to machine-generated knowledge.

Large language models inherit the same received texts and scholarly settlements. They can reproduce the authority of philological decisions without reproducing the arguments through which those decisions were made.

The machine does not necessarily correct the underlying institutional problem. It can make the problem more efficient and pervasive.

[Primary text: §I.5.]

9. What Sharks proposes instead: liberation through inspectability
The essay does not end by demanding that everyone accept the alternative Sappho interpretation.

Its proposed remedy is procedural and epistemological.

Sharks identifies five operations:

Restore the transmitted text, distinguishing what actually survives from editorial reconstruction.

Admit the binding between textual elements as evidence, rather than judging each element in isolation.

Restore Sappho as the maker whose compositional intelligence must be accounted for.

Open the scholarly record, including the competing arguments and the history of editorial decisions.

Leave the final decision to the reader, who can inspect both readings on the same evidentiary scale.

The paired comparison in the companion article, ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ (#1781), is central to this proposal.

Rather than simply substituting one authoritative interpretation for another, Sharks wants to make the competing interpretations inspectable feature by feature.

The aim is to transfer the authority to decide from an institutional gatekeeper to readers who possess the evidence and can evaluate the argument.

That is why the essay's insistence on openness is more than a complaint about subscription costs. It is a claim about the conditions under which intellectual authority can be legitimate.

10. How strong is the argument?
It is worth distinguishing the strongest findings from the more ambitious interpretations.

Claim

Evidentiary status in the essay

Textual questions become less frequent at larger grains

Supported by coded historical material

Relational evidence disproportionately confirms received texts

Supported by the 1906–1922 census

Whole-work verdicts frequently lack an immediately stated ground

Quantitatively supported, with a full-review qualification

The journal's public metadata is unusually closed

Supported by Crossref and OpenAlex comparisons

Canonical authorship is rarely reopened in recent scholarship

Supported by the sampled comparison material, with acknowledged exceptions

The jealousy reading appropriates Sappho's authorship

A substantive interpretive and ethical argument, dependent on the companion article's reading

Classical philology operates colonially

A theoretical interpretation of the documented mechanisms

Decisions circulate uncited as received texts

A hypothesis, not yet directly demonstrated

The author is unusually explicit about the limitations of the research.

Among the open issues are:

The full review texts need further examination to establish whether bare verdicts summarize arguments elsewhere.

Some contemporary material is represented by abstracts rather than full articles.

The historical coding still has outstanding audits.

The citation hypothesis needs to be traced through editions and reference works.

The definition of canonical versus minor authors needs an independently fixed test.

These qualifications matter. The essay is a working research notebook, not a claim that every empirical question has been settled.

There is also a provenance issue worth noting: Sharks identifies the work as human–machine collaborative. The author claims responsibility for the research question, predictions, interpretive rulings, and readings, while Claude performed the harvesting, coding, measurement, auditing, and drafting under direction. The essay discloses this openly, including the tension with Classical Philology's own AI-submission rules.

[Citations for the methodological and provenance qualifications: §§3, 7–9, 11.]

Overall interpretation
I think the most important thing about Dead Letters is that it is making a more fundamental argument than the familiar criticism that classical scholarship is conservative, exclusionary, or insufficiently open to alternative interpretations.

Its argument is about the relationship between the admissibility of evidence and the authority to define an object.

Philology can be meticulous at the level of individual words while remaining insufficiently accountable at the level where those words constitute a poem, an author, or a corpus. Its technical sophistication does not necessarily protect it from institutional prejudice. Indeed, the atomization of evidence can conceal the point at which judgment becomes taste.

Sappho is the decisive example because the stakes become visible in a single poem. The question is not merely whether the jealousy reading or the future-reader reading is correct. It is who gets to determine the terms on which that question can be decided, and whether the maker's own compositional achievement is allowed to count as evidence.

The most radical proposition is therefore the essay's final one:

The authority to decide what an ancient text is should belong not to the institution that happens to control its received form, but to whoever can make the decision openly, with the whole textual record in hand, and answerable to the work itself.

That is what the title's three terms ultimately connect:

Dead letters: scholarship's decisions circulate without the arguments that produced them.

The atom of evidence: a method that can preserve the received whole while appearing to question it.

Who decides what Sappho is: the ethical and political question of who possesses the authority to define the past.

The essay's ultimate demand is not simply a different Sappho. It is a different relationship between scholarship, evidence, institutions, and readers.
